title: The thirteen principles
hook: his list of core Jewish beliefs, in his commentary on Sanhedrin 10

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Commentary on the Mishnah, written on the road, and your line: young and ambitious. Did your long project get its first small step? Today, one of that book's doorways. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-three.

All Israel have a share in the world to come. That, in paraphrase, is how a chapter of the Mishnah, in tractate Sanhedrin, opens. It backs the line with a verse from Isaiah: "Thy people also shall be all righteous." Then it names a few people who lose that share. The Mishnah stops there. It doesn't say what a share is, or what a person has to hold to keep one. Maimonides, working through the Mishnah passage by passage, reaches this chapter and decides the question can't wait. So he writes an answer, and the answer becomes a list. Today, the list.
screen: `A SHARE IN THE WORLD TO COME.` → `THE MISHNAH DOESN'T SAY WHAT IT IS.` → `MAIMONIDES WRITES A LIST.`

segments.voice: The thirteen principles. First, what he called them. Not commandments and not rules. In the Hebrew translation, they are yesodot, foundations, the stones a house stands on. You don't live in the foundation. You live in the house. But without it, the house doesn't stand. Second, the shape of the list. It moves in three stretches. The first five are about God. The next four are about prophecy and the Torah. The last four are about what God knows and does, and what is still to come. Over the next three days, we'll take one stretch a day. Third, why it was new. The Torah gives commandments. The Mishnah gives laws and arguments. Neither one stops to hand you a numbered list of beliefs. Maimonides did, in the middle of a commentary on the oral law, because he thought a person ought to know what the foundations are, not only what to do. Fourth, what came after. Later, his list was set in verse and printed in prayer books, and it was also questioned. Other scholars drew up lists of their own. That argument has a day of its own later this week. For now, notice the move. Faced with a single word in an old text, a share, Maimonides asked what it rests on, and wrote it down so that anyone could read it. Thirteen principles.
screen: `FOUNDATIONS, NOT RULES.` · `THREE STRETCHES: GOD, TORAH, WHAT'S TO COME.` · `A NUMBERED LIST OF BELIEFS.` · `READ, SUNG AND QUESTIONED.` · then, large: `THIRTEEN PRINCIPLES.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to hear the list once, plainly, and then sit. Settle, and let your breath slow. Here it is, in short. God exists. God is one. God has no body. God is eternal. Only God is to be worshiped. The prophets spoke truth. The prophecy of Moses stands apart. The Torah is from heaven. The Torah will not be replaced. God knows what people do. God rewards and punishes. The messiah will come. The dead will live. Don't sort them yet. Notice which line stayed with you. Then let it go, and stay with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The thirteen principles. Maimonides' foundations of Jewish belief, set out in his commentary on the Mishnah's chapter about a share in the world to come. Today's word.
Your line: thirteen principles. Today, come back once to the line from the list that stayed with you, and ask what it might rest on. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Maimonides' thirteen principles are studied in his commentary on Sanhedrin, and versions of them appear in prayer books, both as the poem Yigdal and as a series of lines that each begin "I believe with complete faith."

notes: 'All Israel have a share in the world to come' is given in quotation marks as a common paraphrase of Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1 (the source is marked paraphrase). Editors may prefer to drop the quotation marks.
In some editions the chapter is numbered 11 (Perek Chelek). The script says only 'a chapter of tractate Sanhedrin'; the index says Sanhedrin 10.
'Yesodot' as the Hebrew translation's term for the principles (e.g. 'the first foundation'): please confirm.
The three-stretch grouping (1–5 God; 6–9 prophecy and Torah; 10–13 knowledge, reward, messiah, resurrection) follows the outline's next three days.
'Neither one stops to hand you a numbered list of beliefs' (Torah, Mishnah): please confirm this is fair.
Practice's short list is a summary, not Maimonides' wording.
Yigdal was taught in year two (day 606); it is mentioned only in howItsDone here.
Editor pass: removed quotation marks from the paraphrased Mishnah line in the hook (no public-domain wording); trimmed 'read, sung' from the after-history line.
